analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent a tax break letting businesses immediately deduct half the cost of new equipment.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee approved the bill 24-13 and placed it on the House calendar, but it never received a House floor vote before that Congress ended; a modified version of bonus depreciation was later enacted as part of the December 2015 tax extenders law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make permanent the "bonus depreciation" tax break, which lets businesses deduct 50% of the cost of equipment, machinery, and building improvements in the year they buy it, instead of spreading the deduction over many years. It also adds an extra $8,000 to the annual depreciation cap for cars and lets farmers immediately deduct half the cost of planting fruit and nut trees and vines. Because the bill would permanently reduce federal revenue, it also instructs that its cost not be counted on the budget scorecards used to enforce pay-as-you-go rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that make large capital investments — manufacturers, transport and equipment buyers, commercial landlords and tenants who build out interiors, and orchard and vineyard operators. A permanent deduction is worth the most to companies with large, steady profits to shelter, because it lowers their taxable income right away.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the 50% "bonus depreciation" deduction permanent for qualifying business property placed in service after 2014, instead of letting it expire on schedule.
Raises the first-year depreciation limit on passenger vehicles by $8,000, indexed to inflation, letting buyers of higher-priced vehicles deduct more up front.
Allows farmers to immediately deduct 50% of the cost of fruit and nut trees, vines, and other multi-year plants planted or grafted after 2014.
Expands a corporate election to use accumulated minimum tax credits faster in place of taking bonus depreciation, with the resulting credit made refundable.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. A permanent version of this deduction reduces federal revenue by tens of billions of dollars over ten years, a cost ultimately borne by taxpayers through higher deficits or the need for other taxes or spending cuts. The bill itself includes no offset and directs that its cost not be entered on statutory pay-as-you-go scorecards.

drawbacks.text: Making the deduction permanent removes tens of billions of dollars a year in federal revenue with no offset, and the bill shields itself from the statutory pay-as-you-go enforcement mechanism.

The benefit is concentrated among companies that are already profitable and already planning to invest; businesses with no tax liability in the current year get little from a deduction, so the break flows to the largest and most profitable firms rather than to startups or struggling ones.

Immediate expensing can tilt investment decisions toward tax-favored equipment and away from uses that make more economic sense, and research on earlier temporary versions found only modest effects on overall business investment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is real: letting businesses deduct equipment costs sooner improves cash flow and can modestly encourage investment. But the version reported here converts a temporary stimulus-style provision into a permanent revenue giveaway, weighted toward already-profitable firms, with no offset and a built-in exemption from pay-as-you-go enforcement. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the ten-year cost is large relative to the measurable economic benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The Ways and Means Committee approved it 24-13 and put it on the House calendar, but House leadership never brought it to the floor, and the Congress ended without a vote; a scaled-back version of the underlying tax break passed later that year inside a larger package.

narrative.text: Introduced May 21, 2015 by Rep. Patrick Tiberi with 23 original cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Budget Committees.
The Ways and Means Committee marked it up on September 17, 2015 and ordered it reported with amendments by a vote of 24 to 13.

On October 28, 2015 the committee reported the amended bill (H. Rept. 114-317), the Budget Committee was discharged, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills ready for House floor action.
No floor vote ever followed: the bill sat on the calendar until the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

That December, Congress enacted a modified version of bonus depreciation — permanent but with the 50% rate phased down over several years — inside the broader year-end tax extenders law, rather than as a standalone vote on this bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that would have lost the deduction when it expired gained certainty when a permanent (though phased-down) version was enacted in the December 2015 tax package. For this bill itself, no vote ever happened, so its specific backers gained nothing directly from it; supporters of full permanence had to wait for later legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Equipment-buying businesses; bonus depreciation later became law anyway

for.name: Rep. Patrick J. Tiberi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make bonus depreciation permanent and recruited 23 original cosponsors.

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee
for.role: Tax-writing committee, chaired by Rep. Paul Ryan
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill on September 17, 2015 and ordered it reported with amendments, 24-13.

against.name: 13 Ways and Means Committee members
against.role: Committee members voting no on ordering the bill reported
against.what_they_did: Voted no when the committee approved the bill 24-13.

against.role: House Speaker's office, controls the floor schedule

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsors and 46 of its 50 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Ways and Means Committee approved it 24-13; the record does not break down the committee vote by party, so the exact split is inferred from the bill's overall partisan makeup.

industries.note: Permanent 50% bonus depreciation lets these firms immediately deduct half the cost of new equipment, cutting their tax bills by billions per year. The gain comes from forgone federal revenue, so the cost lands on taxpayers generally.

industries.industry: Passenger vehicle buyers and auto dealers
industries.note: An extra $8,000 of first-year depreciation on cars, indexed to inflation, is worth the most to buyers of higher-priced vehicles, effectively subsidizing luxury and heavy SUV purchases at the Treasury's expense.

industries.industry: Fruit and nut growers, orchards and vineyards
industries.note: Growers can immediately deduct half the cost of planting trees and vines that take years to bear fruit, a targeted break for orchard and vineyard operators paid for with federal revenue.

industries.industry: Commercial real estate and interior-buildout tenants (retail, restaurants, offices)
industries.note: The bill reclassifies leasehold-style interior improvements as 'qualified improvement property' eligible for bonus depreciation, letting tenants and landlords write off buildouts immediately.
